prize_parts.citation: for showing how technological change and import competition reshape labour demand, local labour markets and wage inequality

statement.case_for: B044 combines a conceptual framework (tasks and labour demand) with credible quasi-experimental evidence on trade exposure. That pairing of data discovery and an explanatory framework is the kind of contribution I think the criteria reward. The China-shock design is transparent and has been replicated across countries. It shifted the profession's view of adjustment costs and the distribution of the gains from trade. It also changed policy debate. The core findings are 10 to 20 years old and have been repeatedly stress-tested, and the debate has refined magnitudes rather than overturned the finding. Compared with B002, it has a longer track record. Compared with B040, it rests on direct empirical identification, whereas the empirical validation of the collateral-constraint mechanism is more indirect.
statement.case_against: The strongest reservation is attribution and whether this is one prize-sized achievement. The task framework and the trade-shock evidence are separable strands, with different co-authors, some of whom (Levy, Murnane, Acemoglu) are not credited or are already laureates. The size and persistence of the China-shock effects, and the shift-share inference they rely on, are still actively contested. A three-name limit also excludes Katz, whose skill-biased-change work I credited in my opening ranking.

responses.point: Krusell ranks B002 first. He sees population-scale administrative data as a major measurement advance with causal evidence on neighbourhood exposure, and he thinks a Chetty-Hendren core is cleanest. He still lists B044 second with Autor, Dorn and Hanson.
responses.response: I agree on the merit of B002. I ranked it second myself, and I find the data and identification standards compelling. My difference is on maturity and attribution. Most of the key results are from 2014 onward, and long-run validation of place effects is still emerging. Credit is also spread across a large collaboration. I would not exclude Friedman on the grounds that he is less central, given his data and teacher value-added work. Krusell's second-ranked trio matches where I now land on B044. I keep B002 as an alternative, not the lead, because the track record is shorter.

responses.point: Fredriksson ranks B044 first and proposes Autor and Hanson as the cleanest core. He notes that Dorn and Katz made important contributions that cannot all fit within three names, and he flags identification issues in shift-share designs.
responses.response: I share the first-place assessment and the concern about shift-share inference. I would not drop Dorn. He is a co-author on the central trade-shock papers, and a pair would split a three-author body of work that is unusually cleanly attributable. I now concede that Katz is the weaker fit, and I am revising my opening trio. His skill-bias contribution is real but is an earlier, separate strand, and it would stretch the citation beyond what the three names can credit coherently.

responses.point: Andersson ranks B040 first as a clean two-person award (Kiyotaki and Moore). He sees ample time for judgement. He flags overlap with the 2022 prize on banks and financial crises and notes that empirical validation is mixed. He ranks B044 eighth because it is recent and identification is debated.
responses.response: I accept that B040 has the cleanest attribution of any shortlisted candidate. I ranked it third because of overlap with the 2022 prize and because validation of the mechanism is more indirect. Andersson's own points on weak empirical validation partly support that ranking. On B044, I accept the recency and identification concerns, but a decade of replication across countries and widely shared methods answers much of the first. The debate about magnitudes is real, but it concerns size and persistence, not whether adjustment costs exist. I keep B040 as an alternative but do not place it first.

responses.point: Teorell ranks B017 first and B044 second. He treats the China-shock and task work as influential across fields, including political economy. He notes that Katz would exceed the three-name limit and that Acemoglu, already a laureate, is part of the task-model lineage.
responses.response: His point on Acemoglu and the task lineage is the best argument for centring the citation on the trade-shock and labour-demand evidence, with the task framework as context, and not as a separate claim for the credited names. I agree with him on Katz and the three-name limit. I am less persuaded that B017 should lead. I do not question its merit, but I weigh the 2024 institutions prize's overlap more heavily than he does.

uncertainties: Whether the Committee sees the task framework and the trade-shock evidence as one prize-sized contribution or two, and whether the citation as drafted holds them together without overstating what the three credited names did on tasks.
How much weight to give the ongoing debate over the size and persistence of China-shock effects and the inference in shift-share designs.
Whether excluding Katz is the right call, or whether a Katz-inclusive trio better reflects the technology and wage-inequality strand.
Whether overlap with the 2024 technology-and-institutions prize and the 2023 labour-market prize affects timing or marginal novelty.
I rely on general knowledge of the literature and have not independently verified citation or replication figures.
statement.conflict_note: None apparent from the supplied profile. B044 is close to my field of labour economics, which I note as a possible source of familiarity bias, but my profile lists no co-authorship or institutional tie with any credited person on the shortlist.
